summary: Defines the Path header field for SIP, which lets proxies between a user agent and its registrar record themselves during registration. The registrar can then route later requests back through those proxies, which matters when network topology puts proxies in the way. It was later updated by RFC 5626.

plainLanguage.summary: If a package must go through certain post offices to reach you, the registry should remember them. The Path header leaves a trail of those stops so mail can follow it back.

subtitle: How SIP proxies between a phone and its registrar can leave a trail so later calls find their way back.

tldr.problem: When a SIP user agent registers through one or more proxies, the registrar has no way to learn which proxies later requests must pass through to reach that user agent.
tldr.mechanism: A new Path header field lets each proxy add itself to a REGISTER request. The registrar stores the list, echoes it in the response, and the home proxy later preloads it as a Route on requests heading to the user agent.
tldr.outcome: Requests for a registered user can follow the same chain of proxies back, though the Path is only as trustworthy as the protection around it. RFC 5626 later updated this RFC.

facts.label: Proxy rejection when support is required

today: RFC 3327 is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 5626; it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Registration Routing Problem
sections.content:
In SIP, the REGISTER method mostly ties a temporary contact address to an address-of-record. The contact is usually a URI such as sip:alice@pc33.atlanta.com that tracks the IP address or hostname of the user agent (UA). The trouble is that one or more proxies may sit between the UA and the registrar, and any request travelling from the user's home network to the UA has to cross them.

The RFC's scenario is UA1 - P1 - P2 - P3 - REGISTRAR. UA1 must use P1 as its outbound proxy, and traffic in both directions crosses all three proxies. The registrar, or a closely related home proxy (the terminal point for routing an address-of-record), needs to know which proxies a request must transit to get back. Sometimes SIP routing tables or DNS reveal this. In other cases, such as the one raised by 3GPP, the information is not available outside the REGISTER transaction itself.

The Path header field accumulates and carries that list of proxies. The RFC compares it to Record-Route in dialog-initiating requests. The routing it sets up applies only to requests transiting or originating in the home domain.
sections.plainLanguage: A message sometimes has to go back through the same doors it came in by. Path is a way of writing down those doors on the way in.

sections.title: When the Path Mechanism Applies
sections.content:
The applicability statement says Path is useful when intermediate proxies sit between a UA and its registrar and three conditions hold:

  • One or more of those proxies are visited by registration requests from the UA to the registrar.
  • The same proxies, or a set known to them, must be traversed in reverse order by requests sent through a home proxy to the UA. In the simplest case the route back is the exact inverse of the route in.
  • The network topology is such that the proxies to visit are not implied by SIP routing tables, DNS or similar mechanisms.

If routing tables or DNS already give the answer, there is nothing for Path to add.
sections.plainLanguage: You only need the written trail when the way back is not obvious. If the road home is already marked, you can skip it.

sections.title: The Path Header Field
sections.content:
Path is a SIP extension header field with syntax very similar to Record-Route. It appears in REGISTER requests and in 200-class responses to REGISTER. Any SIP node traversed by the request MAY insert a Path header field. As with Route, separate Path header fields are evaluated in order, and they MAY be combined into one compound header field.

The registrar reflects the accumulated Path into the REGISTER response, and intermediate nodes pass it back to the originating UA. The UA therefore learns which nodes joined its registered path.

The RFC contrasts Path with Record-Route. Path applies to REGISTER and its 200-class responses, where Record-Route is not defined for backward compatibility. Also, a Record-Route vector covers only the dialog that created it, while a Path vector applies to future dialogs.

Path values follow the syntax of a Route element, so they MUST include the loose-routing parameter ;lr for full compliance with SIP. A UA can show support by putting the option tag path in a Supported header field.
sections.plainLanguage: Path looks a lot like the notes a letter already collects as it travels, but it is written on the sign-up form, so it works for all later letters and not just one conversation.

sections.title: Procedures for Each Party
sections.content:
User agent. The UA registers as usual. The response MAY contain a Path header field, and a UA normally ignores it, although it MAY show it to the user. Looking at it can help spot proxies that added themselves inappropriately. The UA SHOULD include the option tag path in all Supported header fields, and SHOULD include a Supported header field in all requests. A UA MAY put a Path header in a request, but the RFC warns this is not broadly applicable and can make the UA be treated like a proxy.

Intermediate proxies. A proxy that wants to be on the path for future requests inserts its own URI as the topmost Path value before forwarding the REGISTER. A proxy SHOULD NOT add Path unless the UA indicated support. If the proxy needs the registrar to support Path and the UA did not say it does, the proxy SHOULD reject the request with a 421 response. Proxies SHOULD NOT alter Path values in the response.

Registrar. For a successful REGISTER with Path, the registrar builds an ordered path vector from the Path values, stores it with the contact and address-of-record, and copies the Path into its 200-class response. If a request has Path but no UA support was indicated, the recommended policy is to reject it with 420 (Bad Extension), which lets the UA notice that a proxy added Path without permission. Some registrars MAY accept it anyway.

Home proxy. It consults the registrar's database, rewrites the request-URI to the registered contact, and now also copies the stored path vector into the Route header field of the outgoing request as a preloaded route. The outgoing request then passes through the proxies recorded at registration. How this combines with local routing policy is implementation dependent.
sections.plainLanguage: Each gate writes its name on the slip. The castle keeper keeps the slip. When a letter arrives for you, the keeper reads the slip out loud and sends the letter through those same gates.

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a registration and a later call. In the registration, UA1 (address 192.0.2.4) sends a REGISTER with Supported: path through P1, P2 and P3 to the registrar. P1 and P3 are configured to add themselves; P2 is not. P1 adds Path: <sip:P1.EXAMPLEVISITED.COM;lr> and P3 adds its own value above that. The 200 OK carries Path: <sip:P3.EXAMPLEHOME.COM;lr>,<sip:P1.EXAMPLEVISITED.COM;lr> back to UA1.

In the later INVITE from UA2, the registrar looks up UA1, replaces the request-URI with the registered Contact, and pushes the stored path vector onto the Route stack. The request goes to P3, then P1, then UA1. The RFC notes that P3 and P1 can each add their own Record-Route entry if they want to stay on the path for the rest of that dialog.
sections.plainLanguage: The slip says gate three, then gate one. When a visitor's letter comes in, the keeper sends it to gate three first, then gate one, and then it reaches you.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says there are few security considerations beyond those in SIP, and that from a security perspective Path is identical to Record-Route. The main risk is an attacker getting a proxy into the Path, because that proxy would then see future calls meant for the UA. This could happen by altering data on the wire or by impersonation (a node insertion attack).

For requests, systems using Path SHOULD use transport-layer protection such as TLS or IPsec for integrity and mutual authentication, and UAs SHOULD use sips: URIs to ask for protection across hops. The registering UA SHOULD also use S/MIME to give the registrar a protected copy of its request, including Supported with path. A registrar that receives such a request MUST honor Path only if support is indicated in the protected header.

For responses, the Path returned to the UA lets it detect node insertion. Registrars returning Path SHOULD attach a signed S/MIME copy of the response, and UAs SHOULD validate it and SHOULD render the Path to the user or check it programmatically.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stranger sneaks onto the list of gates, they could read your mail. So the keeper signs the slip and shows it back to you, and you can check nobody added a name.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC adds two entries to the SIP registries defined in SIP: the header field Path, which has no compact form, and the option tag path. Both are registered against RFC 3327.
sections.plainLanguage: The new name and the new keyword were written into the official lists so nobody else uses them for something different.

data.title: Path header field
data.code:
Path = "Path" HCOLON path-value *( COMMA path-value )
path-value = name-addr *( SEMI rr-param )
